techniques.name: Ridge Regression Surrogates
techniques.description: This technique approximates a complex model by training a ridge regression (a linear model with L2 regularisation) on the original model's predictions. The ridge regression serves as a global surrogate that balances fidelity and interpretability, capturing the main linear relationships that the complex model learned whilst ignoring noise due to regularisation. This approach is particularly useful when stakeholders need to understand the overall behaviour of a complex model through transparent linear coefficients.

example_use_cases.description: Approximating a complex ensemble model used for credit scoring with a ridge regression surrogate to identify the most influential features (income, credit history, debt-to-income ratio) and their linear relationships for regulatory compliance reporting.

Creating a ridge regression surrogate of a neural network used for medical diagnosis to understand which patient symptoms and biomarkers have the strongest linear predictive relationships with disease outcomes.

Creating an interpretable approximation of a complex insurance pricing model for regulatory compliance, enabling stakeholders to understand and validate the decision-making process through transparent linear relationships.

limitations.description: Linear approximation may miss important non-linear relationships and interactions captured by the original complex model.
Requires a representative dataset to train the surrogate model, which may not be available or may be expensive to generate.
Ridge regularisation may oversimplify the model by shrinking coefficients, potentially hiding important but less dominant features.
Surrogate fidelity depends on how well linear relationships approximate the original model's behaviour across the entire input space.

resources.title: Extracting Tree-Structured Representations of Trained Networks
resources.abstract: A  significant  limitation  of  neural  networks  is  that  the  represen(cid:173) tations  they  learn  are  usually  incomprehensible  to  humans.  We  present a  novel algorithm , TREPAN,  for extracting comprehensible,  symbolic representations from  trained neural  networks.  Our algo(cid:173) rithm uses  queries to induce a  decision tree that approximates the  concept  represented by  a  given  network.  Our experiments demon(cid:173) strate that TREPAN is  able to produce decision trees that maintain  a high level of fidelity to their respective networks while being com(cid:173) prehensible  and  accurate.  Unlike  previous  work  in  this  area,  our  algorithm is  general in its applicability and scales well  to large net(cid:173) works  and problems with  high-dimensional input spaces.

resources.title: Interpretable Machine Learning: A Guide for Making Black Box Models Explainable

sample_claims.text: The model's global behavior is approximated by a simpler representation that captures dominant linear relationships across all predictions
The credit scoring model's decision logic can be explained through consistent linear weights applied uniformly across all applicant evaluations
The diagnostic system's predictions are attributable to weighted combinations of patient features that remain stable across the entire population
The environmental forecasting model's feature influences are represented through simplified linear coefficients that prioritize robust patterns over noise
The complex ensemble model's overall decision-making process is captured by an interpretable linear approximation that reveals primary feature contributions

techniques.name: Prototype and Criticism Models
techniques.description: Prototype and Criticism Models provide data understanding by identifying two complementary sets of examples: prototypes represent the most typical instances that best summarise common patterns in the data, whilst criticisms are outliers or edge cases that are poorly represented by the prototypes. For example, in a dataset of customer transactions, prototypes might be the most representative buying patterns (frequent small purchases, occasional large purchases), whilst criticisms could be unusual behaviours (bulk buyers, one-time high-value customers). This dual approach reveals both what is normal and what is exceptional, helping understand data coverage and model blind spots.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing medical imaging datasets to identify prototype scans that represent typical healthy tissue patterns and criticism examples showing rare disease presentations, helping radiologists understand what the model considers 'normal' versus cases requiring special attention.

Evaluating credit scoring models by finding prototype borrowers who represent typical low-risk profiles and criticism cases showing unusual but legitimate financial patterns that the model might misclassify, ensuring fair treatment of edge cases.

Evaluating representation bias in hiring datasets by examining whether prototypes systematically exclude certain demographic groups and criticisms disproportionately represent minorities, revealing data collection inequities.

limitations.description: Selection of prototypes and criticisms is highly dependent on the choice of distance metric or similarity measure, which may not capture all meaningful relationships in the data.
Computational complexity can become prohibitive for very large datasets, as the method often requires pairwise comparisons or optimisation over the entire dataset.
The number of prototypes and criticisms to select is typically a hyperparameter that requires domain expertise to set appropriately.
Results may not generalise well if the training data distribution differs significantly from the deployment data distribution.

resources.title: Examples are not Enough, Learn to Criticize! Criticism for Interpretability
resources.abstract: Example-based explanations are widely used in the effort to improve the interpretability of highly complex distributions. However, prototypes alone are rarely sufficient to represent the gist of the complexity. In order for users to construct better mental models and understand complex data distributions, we also need criticism to explain what are not captured by prototypes. Motivated by the Bayesian model criticism framework, we develop MMD-critic which efficiently learns prototypes and criticism, designed to aid human interpretability. A human subject pilot study shows that the MMD-critic selects prototypes and criticism that are useful to facilitate human understanding and reasoning. We also evaluate the prototypes selected by MMD-critic via a nearest prototype classifier, showing competitive performance compared to baselines.

resources.title: Prototype selection for interpretable classification
resources.abstract: Prototype methods seek a minimal subset of samples that can serve as a distillation or condensed view of a data set. As the size of modern data sets grows, being able to present a domain specialist with a short list of "representative" samples chosen from the data set is of increasing interpretative value. While much recent statistical research has been focused on producing sparse-in-the-variables methods, this paper aims at achieving sparsity in the samples. We discuss a method for selecting prototypes in the classification setting (in which the samples fall into known discrete categories). Our method of focus is derived from three basic properties that we believe a good prototype set should satisfy. This intuition is translated into a set cover optimization problem, which we solve approximately using standard approaches. While prototype selection is usually viewed as purely a means toward building an efficient classifier, in this paper we emphasize the inherent value of having a set of prototypical elements. That said, by using the nearest-neighbor rule on the set of prototypes, we can of course discuss our method as a classifier as well.

sample_claims.text: The medical imaging dataset's coverage is characterised by both typical tissue patterns and rare pathological presentations requiring specialised attention
The credit model's validation set includes both representative borrower profiles and exceptional cases that deviate from standard lending patterns
The environmental monitoring system's training data reflects both common measurement conditions and unusual scenarios that test operational boundaries
The hiring dataset's representative candidates do not systematically exclude particular demographic groups whilst edge cases disproportionately represent minorities
The system's performance on atypical cases is documented alongside its behaviour on prototypical examples

techniques.name: Contrastive Explanation Method
techniques.description: The Contrastive Explanation Method (CEM) explains model decisions by generating contrastive examples that reveal what makes a prediction distinctive. It identifies 'pertinent negatives' (minimal features that could be removed to change the prediction) and 'pertinent positives' (minimal features that must be present to maintain the prediction). This approach helps users understand not just what led to a decision, but what would need to change to achieve a different outcome, providing actionable insights for decision-making.

example_use_cases.description: Explaining loan application rejections by showing that removing recent late payments (pertinent negative) or adding £5,000 more annual income (pertinent positive) would change the decision to approval, giving applicants clear actionable guidance.

Analysing medical diagnosis models by identifying that removing a specific symptom combination would change a high-risk classification to low-risk, helping clinicians understand the critical diagnostic factors.

Providing transparent hiring decisions by showing job candidates exactly which qualifications (pertinent positives) they need to acquire or which application elements (pertinent negatives) might be hindering their success.

limitations.description: Computationally expensive as it requires solving an optimisation problem for each individual instance to find minimal perturbations.
Results can be highly sensitive to hyperparameter settings, requiring careful tuning to produce meaningful explanations.
May generate unrealistic or impossible contrastive examples if constraints are not properly specified, leading to impractical recommendations.
Limited to scenarios where feature perturbations are meaningful and actionable, making it less suitable for immutable characteristics or highly constrained domains.

resources.title: Explanations based on the Missing: Towards Contrastive Explanations with Pertinent Negatives
resources.abstract: In this paper we propose a novel method that provides contrastive explanations justifying the classification of an input by a black box classifier such as a deep neural network. Given an input we find what should be %necessarily and minimally and sufficiently present (viz. important object pixels in an image) to justify its classification and analogously what should be minimally and necessarily \emph{absent} (viz. certain background pixels). We argue that such explanations are natural for humans and are used commonly in domains such as health care and criminology. What is minimally but critically \emph{absent} is an important part of an explanation, which to the best of our knowledge, has not been explicitly identified by current explanation methods that explain predictions of neural networks. We validate our approach on three real datasets obtained from diverse domains; namely, a handwritten digits dataset MNIST, a large procurement fraud dataset and a brain activity strength dataset. In all three cases, we witness the power of our approach in generating precise explanations that are also easy for human experts to understand and evaluate.

resources.title: Contrastive Explanations Method (CEM) applied to MNIST — Alibi Explain
Understanding How CNNs Recognize Facial Expressions: A Case Study with LIME and CEM
resources.abstract: Recognizing facial expressions has been a persistent goal in the scientific community. Since the rise of artificial intelligence, convolutional neural networks (CNN) have become popular to recognize facial expressions, as images can be directly used as input. Current CNN models can achieve high recognition rates, but they give no clue about their reasoning process. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has been developed as a means to help to interpret the results obtained by machine learning models. When dealing with images, one of the most-used XAI techniques is LIME. LIME highlights the areas of the image that contribute to a classification. As an alternative to LIME, the CEM method appeared, providing explanations in a way that is natural for human classification: besides highlighting what is sufficient to justify a classification, it also identifies what should be absent to maintain it and to distinguish it from another classification. This study presents the results of comparing LIME and CEM applied over complex images such as facial expression images. While CEM could be used to explain the results on images described with a reduced number of features, LIME would be the method of choice when dealing with images described with a huge number of features.

sample_claims.text: The model's decision rationale identifies both what features must be present to maintain the current prediction and what features could be removed to change it
The loan application system communicates to applicants the minimal changes needed to reverse a rejection decision
The diagnostic model explains high-risk classifications by identifying which symptom combinations, if absent, would result in a low-risk assessment
The hiring system provides candidates with actionable feedback specifying which qualifications are sufficient for selection and which deficiencies drive rejection
The fraud detection model distinguishes between transactions by showing what transaction attributes would need to be different to flip the fraud classification

techniques.name: ANCHOR
techniques.description: ANCHOR generates high-precision if-then rules that explain individual predictions by identifying the minimal set of feature conditions that guarantee a specific prediction with high confidence. It searches for 'anchor' conditions (e.g., 'age > 30 AND income < £50k') that ensure the model gives the same prediction at least 95% of the time when those conditions are met. This creates human-readable rules that users can trust as sufficient conditions for understanding why a particular decision was made.

example_use_cases.description: Explaining loan application decisions with rules like 'IF credit_score > 650 AND debt_ratio < 0.4 THEN approval = 95% likely', giving applicants clear, actionable conditions they can understand and potentially improve.

Generating diagnostic rules for medical predictions such as 'IF fever > 38.5°C AND white_blood_cells > 12,000 THEN infection = 92% likely', helping clinicians validate automated diagnoses with trusted clinical indicators.

Creating transparent hiring decisions with rules like 'IF experience >= 3_years AND degree = relevant THEN hire = 89% likely', providing clear justification for recruitment decisions that can be audited for fairness.

limitations.description: Limited to local explanations for individual instances, cannot provide global insights about overall model behaviour.
Requires discretisation of continuous features, which can lose important nuanced information and create arbitrary thresholds.
May fail to find suitable anchor rules if precision requirements are too strict or if the prediction space is highly complex.
Computationally expensive as it requires extensive sampling to validate rule precision, especially for high-dimensional data.

resources.title: Anchors: High-Precision Model-Agnostic Explanations
resources.abstract: We introduce a novel model-agnostic system that explains the behavior of complex models with high-precision rules called anchors, representing local, "sufficient" conditions for predictions. We propose an algorithm to efficiently compute these explanations for any black-box model with high-probability guarantees. We demonstrate the flexibility of anchors by explaining a myriad of different models for different domains and tasks. In a user study, we show that anchors enable users to predict how a model would behave on unseen instances with less effort and higher precision, as compared to existing linear explanations or no explanations.

resources.title: Interpretability in HealthCare A Comparative Study of Local Machine Learning Interpretability Techniques
resources.abstract: Although complex machine learning models (e.g., Random Forest, Neural Networks) are commonly outperforming the traditional simple interpretable models (e.g., Linear Regression, Decision Tree), in the healthcare domain, clinicians find it hard to understand and trust these complex models due to the lack of intuition and explanation of their predictions. With the new General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the importance for plausibility and verifiability of the predictions made by machine learning models has become essential. To tackle this challenge, recently, several machine learning interpretability techniques have been developed and introduced. In general, the main aim of these interpretability techniques is to shed light and provide insights into the predictions process of the machine learning models and explain how the model predictions have resulted. However, in practice, assessing the quality of the explanations provided by the various interpretability techniques is still questionable. In this paper, we present a comprehensive experimental evaluation of three recent and popular local model agnostic interpretability techniques, namely, LIME, SHAP and Anchors on different types of real-world healthcare data. Our experimental evaluation covers different aspects for its comparison including identity, stability, separability, similarity, execution time and bias detection. The results of our experiments show that LIME achieves the lowest performance for the identity metric and the highest performance for the separability metric across all datasets included in this study. On average, SHAP has the smallest average time to output explanation across all datasets included in this study. For detecting the bias, SHAP enables the participants to better detect the bias.

sample_claims.text: The model's individual predictions are supported by verifiable sufficient conditions with quantified confidence guarantees
The lending system provides loan applicants with specific, actionable conditions that guarantee approval with stated probability
The diagnostic system's recommendations are justified by minimal sets of clinical indicators that ensure the decision under specified conditions
The hiring decision criteria are documented as precise if-then rules with empirically validated confidence bounds
The fraud detection system identifies sufficient feature combinations that reliably predict flagged transactions with quantified precision

techniques.name: RuleFit
techniques.description: RuleFit creates interpretable surrogate models that can explain complex black-box models or serve as interpretable alternatives. It works by learning a sparse linear model that combines automatically extracted decision rules with original features. The technique first builds tree ensembles to generate candidate rules, then uses LASSO regression to select the most important rules and features. The resulting model provides global explanations through human-readable rules (e.g., 'IF age > 50 AND income < 30k THEN ...') combined with linear feature weights, making complex model behaviour transparent and auditable.

example_use_cases.description: Building customer churn prediction models with rules like 'IF contract_length < 12_months AND support_calls > 5 THEN churn_risk = high', allowing marketing teams to understand and act on the key drivers of customer attrition.

Creating credit scoring models that combine traditional linear factors (income, age) with interpretable rules (IF recent_missed_payments = 0 AND account_age > 2_years THEN creditworthy), providing transparent lending decisions.

Developing regulatory-compliant medical diagnosis models where treatment recommendations combine clinical measurements with clear decision rules (IF blood_pressure > 140 AND diabetes = true THEN high_risk), enabling audit trails for healthcare decisions.

limitations.description: Can generate large numbers of rules even with regularisation, potentially overwhelming users and reducing practical interpretability.
Performance may be inferior to complex ensemble methods when rule complexity is constrained for interpretability.
Rule extraction quality depends heavily on the underlying tree ensemble, which may miss important feature interactions if not properly configured.
Requires careful hyperparameter tuning to balance between model complexity and interpretability, with no universal optimal setting.

resources.title: Predictive learning via rule ensembles
resources.abstract: General regression and classification models are constructed as linear combinations of simple rules derived from the data. Each rule consists of a conjunction of a small number of simple statements concerning the values of individual input variables. These rule ensembles are shown to produce predictive accuracy comparable to the best methods. However, their principal advantage lies in interpretation. Because of its simple form, each rule is easy to understand, as is its influence on individual predictions, selected subsets of predictions, or globally over the entire space of joint input variable values. Similarly, the degree of relevance of the respective input variables can be assessed globally, locally in different regions of the input space, or at individual prediction points. Techniques are presented for automatically identifying those variables that are involved in interactions with other variables, the strength and degree of those interactions, as well as the identities of the other variables with which they interact. Graphical representations are used to visualize both main and interaction effects.

resources.title: RuleFit-Based Nomogram Using Inflammatory Indicators for Predicting Survival in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma, a Bi-Center Study
resources.abstract: Purpose: Traditional prognostic studies utilized different cut-off values, without evaluating potential information contained in inflammation-related hematological indicators. Using the interpretable machine-learning algorithm RuleFit, this study aimed to explore valuable inflammatory rules reflecting prognosis in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) patients. Patients and Methods: In total, 1706 biopsy-proven NPC patients treated in two independent hospitals (1320 and 386) between January 2010 and March 2014 were included. RuleFit was used to develop risk-predictive rules using hematological indicators with no distributive difference between the two centers. Time-event-dependent hematological rules were further selected by stepwise multivariate Cox analysis. Combining high-efficiency hematological rules and clinical predictors, a final model was established. Models based on other algorithms (AutoML, Lasso) and clinical predictors were built for comparison, as well as a reported nomogram. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and concordance index (C-index) were used to verify the predictive precision of different models. A site-based app was established for convenience. Results: RuleFit identified 22 combined baseline hematological rules, achieving AUROCs of 0.69 and 0.64 in the training and validation cohorts, respectively. By contrast, the AUROCs of the optimal contrast model based on AutoML were 1.00 and 0.58. For overall survival, the final model had a much higher C-index than the base model using TN staging in two cohorts (0.769 vs 0.717, P < 0.001; 0.752 vs 0.688, P < 0.001), and showing great generalizability in training and validation cohorts. The two models based on RuleFit rules performed best, compared with other models. As for other endpoints, the final model showed a similar trend. Kaplan–Meier curve exhibited 22.9% (390/1706) patients were “misclassified” by AJCC staging, but the final model could assess risk classification accurately. Conclusion: The proposed final models based on inflammation-related rules based on RuleFit showed significantly elevated predictive performance.

sample_claims.text: The credit risk model's decision logic is expressible as a sparse set of interpretable if-then rules combined with linear feature weights
The patient risk stratification system's predictions are traceable to explicit clinical decision rules that mirror diagnostic reasoning patterns
The fraud detection model identifies risk through comprehensible rules that stakeholders can validate against domain knowledge
The customer churn prediction system's global behavior is approximated by a small number of actionable business rules rather than opaque feature interactions
The regulatory compliance model combines human-readable decision boundaries with weighted factors in a single auditable representation

techniques.name: STRIDE-AI Threat Modelling
techniques.description: STRIDE-AI is a threat-modelling method for machine-learning (ML) systems, proposed by Mauri and Damiani (2021, extended 2022), that lists, before any testing, the ways an attacker could compromise each asset of an ML pipeline and how serious each would be. It adapts Microsoft's STRIDE scheme, in which each of six threat types (spoofing, tampering, repudiation, information disclosure, denial of service and elevation of privilege) breaks one security property (authenticity, integrity, non-repudiation, confidentiality, availability and authorisation), and gives each property an ML-specific definition: confidentiality, for example, means that querying a model reveals nothing beyond its inputs and outputs. The analyst surveys the assets produced across the ML life cycle, such as raw, labelled and validation data, hyperparameters, trained and deployed models and the model architecture, and with each asset's owners runs a failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA, a structured review of how a component could fail and with what effect), answering set questions about how the asset could fail, be misused or be abused. Each failure mode is mapped to the properties it would break and so to STRIDE threats, using the method's published tables of asset types, properties and known attacks; the analyst then works with developers to draw threat trees showing the conditions under which each threat could be realised, and rates each threat's priority (the worked example uses DREAD, which scores five factors from 1 to 10). The output is a threat model, a table of assets, threatened properties, threats and priorities with their threat trees: the method attacks and measures nothing, and choosing and testing controls for the threats it finds is left to other techniques.

example_use_cases.description: The security architect for a solar-farm operator's fault-prediction service, which trains on sensor readings streamed from plant data loggers to an external ML platform, maps each asset to its threatened properties. The threat trees show that the loggers' signatures stop injected readings but not label flipping, because labels are added later on the operator's own platform, so that threat is ranked and passed to the platform team.

Before buying a third-party chest X-ray triage model, a hospital's information-security team runs STRIDE-AI over the vendor's pipeline documentation: training data, the supplied model file, the inference service and the results sent to radiologists. Threats such as tampering with the model file and disclosure of training images through model outputs set the scope of the security tests and contract terms the hospital asks the vendor to meet.

A bank's model-security lead repeats the analysis when a card-fraud model moves from monthly retraining to online learning on live transactions. The transaction stream becomes a training-data asset that anyone making transactions can influence, so tampering with it to drift the model is added as a threat, rated and entered in the bank's risk register.

limitations.description: A finished threat model is not evidence that no other threats exist. Its coverage depends on the asset survey and on what the analysts know; the authors state that ML vulnerabilities cannot be fully enumerated in one pass and that failure modes must be updated as the system and known attacks change, and a 2006 Microsoft account of STRIDE notes there is no well-established way to measure a threat model's quality. Claims should state what was in scope and when the analysis was last revised.

STRIDE-AI identifies and ranks threats but does not choose or test controls. Both papers' abstracts say it guides control selection, but neither gives a procedure: the 2021 paper puts control selection outside its scope and the 2022 paper leaves it to future work, noting that no security control framework designed for ML was available. A claim that the threats are mitigated needs separate evidence, such as attack tests against each control and a control catalogue taken from another source.

Priorities are expert judgements. The worked example uses DREAD scores, which the authors note can give inconsistent results between raters and are no longer recommended as the only basis for ranking. Two teams may rank the same threats differently, so claims that rest on the ranking are stronger when several people score independently or a published severity scale such as a bug bar is used.

The mapping from failure modes to properties and threats is done by hand for every asset, and needs asset owners, developers and a security analyst together. Later work describes it as lacking automation, which limits how far it scales to large pipelines; each significant change, such as moving a model to online learning, means repeating part of the analysis.

The published catalogue of assets, failure modes and known attacks was built in 2021-22 around the life cycle of a conventionally trained model, from requirements to maintenance. It does not list assets specific to language-model applications and agents, such as system prompts, retrieval corpora or connected tools, so analysts of those systems must add the assets and their threats themselves, without guidance from the method.

techniques.name: Fault Tree Analysis
techniques.description: Fault tree analysis (FTA) is a deductive, top-down method that starts from one undesired system-level event, such as an automated braking function failing to brake for an obstacle, and works backwards to the combinations of lower-level events that could cause it. The analyst builds a tree of logic gates beneath that top event: an OR gate means any one of its inputs is enough to cause the event above it, an AND gate means all of its inputs must occur together, and the branches end in basic events such as a hardware failure, a human error or a software error. Solving the tree gives its minimal cut sets, the smallest combinations of basic events that produce the top event (a set with a single event is a single point of failure), and, when each basic event has a probability, the probability of the top event, which can be checked against a target or used to set a probability budget for each part. In a system with a machine-learning component, the model's errors enter the tree as basic events of their own, which unlike random hardware failures happen during normal operation at a rate that has to be measured on test or operational data, often depend on conditions such as weather or occlusion that can be added beneath it as conditioning events, and can be correlated from one input to the next. Working down from an acceptable top-event probability turns the model's share into a budget for its error rate, which becomes a performance requirement on the model; the tree shows where model errors matter in the system and how much error it can tolerate, but not why the model makes them.

example_use_cases.description: An avionics team designing an emergency braking system for taxiing aircraft, in which a neural network detects 'No Entry' signs, builds a quantitative fault tree for loss of the restricted-area alert, budgets the detector's misses beside the hardware failures, converts that budget into a maximum per-frame miss probability for the network, and checks on recorded taxi data whether misses in successive frames are independent, as the calculation assumes.

A driving-automation developer analysing the top event 'object not detected in time' adds weather, occlusion and lighting as triggering conditions beneath the camera detector's miss event. Quantifying the tree with rates measured on its own test drives shows which conditions dominate, and it uses the result to decide where a second sensor is needed before widening the vehicle's operating domain.

A hospital pharmacy planning to add a machine-learning dose checker beside pharmacist review draws a tree for 'harmful overdose reaches the patient', with an AND gate requiring both the checker and the pharmacist to miss the error. The analysis shows the claimed risk reduction holds only if the two misses are independent, so the team plans an audit of whether pharmacists check less carefully once the checker is live.

limitations.description: The tree explains only the top events the analysts choose and the causes they think of. Hazards nobody posed as a top event, and losses that arise from interactions between parts that each worked as specified, do not appear, so a fault tree needs a prior hazard identification to decide which top events matter.

A probability for a model-error event is only as good as the data it was measured on. A miss rate estimated on test data holds for the conditions and input mix in that data and changes when the operating environment shifts, so the top-event probability can be badly wrong in conditions the test set under-represents. The main aerospace safety-assessment guidance gives no method for such performance failures, so each assessment has to justify its own.

Quantifying a tree usually assumes basic events are independent, and machine-learning errors often are not: misses on successive camera frames are correlated, and one condition such as fog can degrade a model and the sensor or person meant to back it up at the same time. Unmodelled dependence makes an AND gate look far more protective than it is, so dependence must be checked on data or modelled explicitly.

The model appears in the tree as one or a few basic events, so the analysis says how often the model may err and where its errors matter, not why it errs or which inputs cause the errors. The triggering conditions added beneath a model-error event are only those the analysts already suspect, and finding others needs analysis of the model and its data.

Building and maintaining a tree for a large system is laborious, and it must be revised whenever the architecture or the model changes. Quantification needs a probability for every basic event, and for software, human and model events those numbers are often unavailable or disputed; aviation software guidance, for example, does not accept software reliability rates in the system safety assessment.

techniques.name: Machine Learning Failure Mode and Effects Analysis
techniques.description: Machine Learning Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (ML FMEA) applies the process form of failure mode and effects analysis, a long-established worksheet method in which a team lists what could go wrong at each step of a process, rates each failure and acts on the worst first, to the pipeline that produces a machine-learning model rather than to the model alone. The team works through the pipeline one step at a time (in the 2025 reference version: collect data requests, collect data, ingest data, validate data, preprocess data, train, tune, analyse, deploy and validate the model, and analyse feedback from the field) and, prompted by guide words such as missing, incorrect or too late, records for each step how the resulting model could fail, the effect on the wider system, the pipeline causes, and the current practices that would prevent or catch the failure. Each row is rated for severity, occurrence and detection, and the product of the three, the risk priority number, ranks the rows so that recommended actions and owners go to the highest risks first; severity is taken from the system-level hazard analysis, because the harm a model failure can do depends on the system it sits in. The method's authors publish a pre-populated template listing typical failure modes, causes and mitigations for each step, which a team tailors to its own model and application. The result is a worksheet of ranked pipeline failure modes, their controls and assigned actions, kept up to date as the pipeline changes; it looks at failures one at a time in how the model is built and does not by itself analyse how the deployed system behaves.

example_use_cases.description: An autonomous-trucking company's perception team fills in the template for its lane-detection model before each major retraining. One row under 'collect data' records that data gathered in a single season could leave the model unable to see faded or snow-covered markings; its severity comes from the vehicle-level hazard analysis, and it leads to an action, with an owner and a date, to constrain data requests by season and weather before release.

A medical-imaging company preparing a chest X-ray triage model for regulatory review uses the worksheet to show its assessors where the pipeline's controls sit. High-ranked rows include training labels taken from a single radiologist's reading, which could teach the model to miss small nodules, mitigated by double reading of a labelled sample, and online learning in deployment, mitigated by switching it off.

After a warehouse robot's object detector starts misclassifying a new kind of shrink-wrapped pallet, the vendor's safety engineer returns to the worksheet, finds that the 'analyse model feedback' step had no control for new packaging reaching customer sites, adds drift monitoring and a trigger for new data requests, and re-rates the affected rows.

limitations.description: It considers one failure mode at a time, step by step, so it does not show how failures in different steps combine, or how a model that meets its specification can still contribute to an accident through its interaction with people and other parts of the system. Teams that need those combinations and interactions have to pair it with a system-level analysis.

Severity, occurrence and detection are judgements on ordinal scales, and there is little data on how often an ML pipeline failure occurs or how reliably a control catches it. The method's authors introduced ML-specific rating criteria in 2026 because traditional FMEA criteria proved ambiguous for ML development; the public template, last updated in April 2025, has no rating criteria, so teams must set and record their own.

It analyses how the model is built, not how it behaves in use: a complete worksheet shows that known pipeline failure modes have controls, not that the deployed model performs safely. Severity has to come from a system-level hazard analysis, so the method cannot stand alone, and its authors present it as one part of a safety management system and safety case.

The pre-populated template makes a quick start but invites teams to tick through the listed failure modes instead of looking for ones specific to their system. Its examples come mostly from autonomous-vehicle development, so teams in other domains, or with other kinds of model such as language models, must add their own failure modes; the 2026 revision added steps for problem definition and for building ground truth or reward signals.

Published evidence that the method finds failures other methods miss is limited. The 2025 paper that introduced it gave no applied example, and the 2026 follow-up reporting applications to autonomous vehicles and humanoid robots is led by the method's originators: four of its twelve authors, including the first author, wrote the 2025 paper, so no independent group has yet reported using it.

sample_claims.text: Every step of the lane-detection model's development pipeline has been analysed for failure modes, and each failure mode ranked above the agreed action limit has an implemented mitigation with a named owner.
Severity ratings in the triage model's ML FMEA are taken from the system-level hazard analysis, so each pipeline risk is rated by its possible effect on patients before it is ranked.
Collection and labelling of the perception model's training data are covered by a documented control for each failure mode identified in the ML FMEA, including seasonal and weather coverage.
Following the field incident, the ML FMEA was revised to add the missing control for unseen packaging types, and the affected failure modes were re-rated.

techniques.name: System-Theoretic Process Analysis
techniques.description: System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) is a hazard analysis method developed by Nancy Leveson at MIT that treats safety as a control problem: a loss can occur when parts of a system that have not failed interact unsafely, for example when a controller acts on a wrong belief about the process it controls. The analysis has four steps: define the losses to prevent and the system-level hazards that lead to them; model the system as a control structure of controllers, the control actions they issue and the feedback they receive; identify unsafe control actions; and write loss scenarios explaining how each could arise. An unsafe control action is one of four types (not providing an action causes a hazard, providing it causes a hazard, providing it too early, too late or in the wrong order, or stopping it too soon or applying it too long), and loss scenarios cover causes such as missing or wrong feedback, a flawed control algorithm, or a controller's process model (its internal picture of what it controls) that no longer matches reality. In a system with machine-learning components, a learned model appears in the control structure as a controller whose control algorithm and process model were learned from data, or as a feedback source, such as a perception model, whose errors mislead a controller; loss scenarios include training data that missed an operating condition, a shift from training to deployment conditions, and operators who over-rely on the model, and published adaptations also model data collection, training and evaluation as control loops, so that a scenario can trace an unsafe control action back to a development decision such as an incomplete reward function. The output is a traceable set of unsafe control actions, loss scenarios and the safety constraints and requirements derived from them, which the team uses to change the design and to decide what to test; it analyses a model of the system before or alongside testing, and it gives no probabilities.

example_use_cases.description: An automotive supplier building a pedestrian collision-avoidance function around a neural-network detector models the vehicle's control structure with the detector as the braking controller's source of feedback. It finds the unsafe control action 'emergency braking not applied while a pedestrian is crossing', with scenarios such as missed detections of partly hidden pedestrians at dusk, and turns them into requirements on training-data coverage and on the detector's miss rate.

A hospital's patient-safety team preparing to deploy a machine-learning early-warning score for patient deterioration models the score, the nurses who receive its alerts and the doctors who act on them as one control structure. It finds unsafe control actions such as an escalation that comes too late because vital signs reach the record in batches, and alerts ignored after repeated false alarms, and changes data entry and the alerting rules before go-live.

A frontier AI developer's safety team analysing internal use of an AI coding agent models the engineers who prompt it, the automated monitor that scores its sessions, the human reviewers and the merge gate as controllers of the company codebase. It finds unsafe control actions such as a monitoring alert that arrives after the agent's change has been merged, and sets requirements on how quickly sessions are reviewed and on reviewers' independence from the agent.

An engineering team training a reinforcement-learning policy to land a drone splits the mission into approach, descent and touchdown, identifies unsafe control actions for each phase, such as descending too fast close to the landing pad, and uses the loss scenarios to choose the wind and sensor-noise perturbations for its simulation tests and to adjust the reward before the next round of training.

limitations.description: The analysis depends on judgement at every step: deciding which losses matter, where the system ends, which parts act as controllers and which scenarios to record. Separate teams analysing the same system can reach different models and scenario lists, so the work needs review by people outside the team, and a short list of loss scenarios is not evidence that no others exist.

STPA does not estimate how likely a hazard or scenario is, and its authors argue that such estimates are unreliable for software-intensive systems. Where an assurance case or regulator needs a quantitative target, such as a failure rate per hour, it must be paired with a quantitative method, and STPA alone cannot show that a scenario is too rare to need a mitigation.

For a learned component the analysts cannot read the process model or the control algorithm, because both are encoded in trained weights. Scenarios explaining why the model would act unsafely are therefore hypotheses about its training data and operating conditions until tests or monitoring confirm them, and for policies with continuous states and actions the analysis has to be split by mission phase or subtask to stay manageable.

A control structure that covers only the system in operation misses causes that lie in how the model was built, such as data collection, labelling, reward design or the choice of evaluation set; a survey of 31 studies applying STPA to learning-enabled systems found that most modelled operation only. Adding the development lifecycle as control loops finds these causes but makes the analysis substantially larger.

A full analysis of a complex system takes sustained effort from people trained in the method, working with domain and machine-learning experts. A language model can draft loss scenarios faster, but its drafts steer the team towards the scenarios it happens to suggest and can leave gaps, so they need the same review as scenarios written by hand.

sample_claims.text: Each unsafe control action identified for the emergency braking controller, including those caused by missed detections from the pedestrian detector, is traced to a safety constraint and to a verified requirement on the detector or the vehicle.

The hazard analysis of the early-warning score covered the clinicians who act on its alerts and the data feeds it depends on as well as the model, and every loss scenario it found has a mitigation recorded in the deployment plan.

Unsafe control actions arising from late or missing review of the coding agent's sessions were identified, and each has a design constraint that bounds the time between an agent's action and its review.
Each loss scenario derived for the drone-landing policy's approach, descent and touchdown phases is covered by at least one simulation test case.
